intro: Use the **past simple** for a **finished** time in the past: *I **went** to Paris **in 2019**.*
Use the **present perfect** when the time is **not finished** or **not important**, or when the past connects to **now**: *I**'ve been** to Paris three times. She**'s lived** here **since** 2015.*

rows: finished time: *yesterday, last week, in 2019, two years ago*
unfinished time: *today, this week, so far, since, for* (until now)
a specific past moment: *When did you arrive?*
life experience, no time given: *Have you ever been to Japan?*
finished period: *He lived in Italy for ten years* (he doesn't now)
period up to now: *He's lived in Canada for ten years* (he still does)
people who are dead: *Shakespeare wrote 37 plays.*
people who are alive, life so far: *She's written three books.*

blocks.md: Never use the present perfect with a finished time expression: *I **saw** him yesterday* (not *I have seen him yesterday*).

With *just, already* and *yet*, American English often uses the past simple (*I just ate*), while British English prefers the present perfect (*I've just eaten*). Both are correct. See [Present Perfect with For, Since, Just, Yet, Already](/blog/grammar/present-perfect-for-since-just-yet-already/).

topics.h1: Present Perfect with For, Since, Just, Yet, Already
intro: We often use the **present perfect** (have/has + past participle) with **for** and **since** to say how long something has continued up to now: *I**'ve lived** here **for** ten years.*
We use it with **just, already** and **yet** to talk about recent actions and things we expect to happen: *She**'s just** left. Have you finished **yet**?*

rows: for ten minutes, for two weeks, for a long time, for ages
a point in time (when it started)
since 9 o'clock, since Monday, since 2015, since I was a child

items.text: I**'ve known** Maria **for** five years.
I**'ve known** Maria **since** 2021.
He**'s worked** here **since** he left university.

blocks.md: Ask with **How long…?**: *How long **have** you **had** your car?* Don't use the present simple: *I**'ve lived** here for years.* (not *I live here for years*)
With *for* and *since*, the situation is still true now. If it has finished, use the past simple: *I **lived** in Rome for two years.* (I don't live there now.)

rows: between have/has and the past participle
between have/has and the past participle, or at the end
until now (we expect it to happen)
at the end of negatives and questions

blocks.md: **Still** + negative means something hasn't happened, and we're surprised or impatient: *He **still** hasn't replied.*
**American and British English:** Americans often use the past simple with *just, already* and *yet*: *I just had lunch. Did you eat yet?* Both styles are correct in their variety.
*She**'s gone** to Paris.* = She is in Paris now. *She**'s been** to Paris.* = She went to Paris and came back.

intro: We use the **present perfect continuous** (have/has been + verb-ing) for an activity that started in the past and is **still continuing**, or that has **just stopped** and we can see the result: *I**'ve been waiting** for an hour. You're wet! **Have** you **been running**?*

sections.h2: How to form the present perfect continuous

items: An activity from the past until now, often with *for, since* or *how long*: *They**'ve been living** here since 2020.*
A recent activity with a result we can see now: *Your eyes are red. **Have** you **been crying**?*
Repeated actions over a period up to now: *I**'ve been going** to the gym a lot recently.*

sections.h2: Present perfect continuous or present perfect simple?

rows: focus on the activity and how long
focus on the result, or how many / how much
*I**'ve been reading** this book for two hours.*
*I**'ve read** 50 pages. I**'ve finished** the book.*

blocks.md: With a number or an amount, use the simple form: *I**'ve drunk** three coffees today.* (not *I've been drinking three coffees*)

State verbs (*know, like, have* = own, *believe, understand*) use the simple form: *I**'ve known** her for years.* (not *I've been knowing*) With *live, work, study* and *teach*, both forms are often possible: *I've lived / I've been living here for five years.*

intro: We use the **past perfect** (had + past participle) for something that happened **before** another past action: *When I arrived, the film **had** already **started**.*
In stories we use it together with the **past simple** (the main events) and the **past continuous** (the background).

sections.h2: How to form the past perfect

blocks.md: In speech, *had* is often **'d**: *I'd forgotten. They'd gone.*

sections.h2: When do we use the past perfect?

items: For the earlier of two past actions: *I couldn't get in because I **had lost** my keys.*
With *already, just, never, before* and *by the time*: *By the time we got there, the shop **had closed**.*

blocks.md: When the order is already clear (for example with *after* or *before*), the past simple is often enough: *After I **finished** work, I went home.* / *After I **had finished** work…* Both are correct.

rows: *Someone **had left** it there the night before.*

blocks.md: *It **was raining** when I **got** home. I **was** tired because I **had worked** for twelve hours. While I **was making** dinner, the phone **rang**. It was my sister. She **had** just **heard** some amazing news.*
The tense changes the order of events: *When I arrived, the film **started**.* (I arrived, then the film started.) *When I arrived, the film **had started**.* (The film started before I arrived.)

intro: We use **used to** + base verb for past habits and past states that are **not true now**: *I **used to play** football every weekend.* (I don't now.) *She **used to live** in Paris.* (She doesn't live there now.)
*Used to* only talks about the past. There is no present form.

rows: We **used to go** camping every summer.
Yes, + subject + did. / No, + subject + didn't.
Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.

blocks.md: After *did* and *didn't*, write **use to** (no d): *didn't **use** to, Did you **use** to…?* You will also see *didn't used to* in informal writing, but *didn't use to* is the standard form.
*Used to* sounds like *yoos-ta*. The d is not pronounced.

sections.h2: When do we use used to?

items: Past habits (repeated actions): *I **used to take** the bus to school.*
Past states: *There **used to be** a cinema here. He **used to be** very shy.*

blocks.md: We don't normally use *used to* for one action, or to say how many times or how long something happened. Use the past simple: *I **went** to Rome in 2019. I **lived** there for ten years.*
For present habits, use the present simple, often with *usually*: *I **usually** walk to work.* (not *I use to walk to work*)
For past **habits**, you can also use **would**: *Every summer, we **would** go to the lake.* But don't use *would* for past **states**: *I **used to have** a dog.* (not *I would have a dog*)

topics.h1: Be Able To (vs Can and Could)
intro: **Be able to** means the same as *can*: *I **can** swim = I **am able to** swim.*
We need it because *can* has only two forms (*can* and *could*). For other tenses and structures, we use **be able to**: *I**'ll be able to** help you tomorrow.*

rows: You**'ll be able to** speak English fluently soon.
I **haven't been able to** sleep well recently.
I'd love **to be able to** play the guitar.
**Being able to** drive is very useful.
after modals: **might / must / should be able to**
He **might be able to** help you.

blocks.md: Never put two modals together: *I **will be able to** drive* (not *I will can drive*).
For a **general ability** in the past, use *could* or *was able to*: *When I was young, I **could** run very fast.*
For **one specific situation** where someone succeeded, use **was / were able to** (or *managed to*), not *could*: *The fire spread quickly, but everyone **was able to** escape.*
In the **negative**, both are fine: *I **couldn't** / **wasn't able to** finish the test.*
With verbs of the senses and thinking, *could* is normal even for one situation: *I **could see** the sea from my room. I **could understand** everything.*

topics.h1: Modals of Deduction: Must, Might, Can't
intro: We use **must, might, may, could** and **can't** to make guesses (deductions) about what is true now, based on the information we have: *She's not answering. She **must be** busy. He **might be** at the gym. That **can't be** Tom; he's in Paris.*

She **might be** at home. / She **may be** at home. / She **could be** at home.
it's possible that it isn't true
That **can't be** the right answer. It doesn't make sense.

blocks.md: For a negative deduction, British English uses **can't**: *He **can't** be hungry; he's just eaten.* In American English, **must not** is also common: *He must not be hungry.*

items: modal + base verb: *She must **know** him.*
modal + be + adjective, noun or place: *They might **be** at work.*
modal + be + -ing for something happening now: *He can't **be sleeping**; the light is on.*

blocks.md: Don't use *to* after these modals, and don't add -s: *She **must be*** (not *must to be*), *He **might** know* (not *mights*).

*You **must** wear a seatbelt.* = a rule (obligation). *You **must** be Anna's sister. You look just like her!* = a deduction. For obligation, see [Must, Have To and Should](/blog/grammar/must-have-to-should/).
*Can* is for general possibility, not for guesses about one situation now: *It **might** be true* (not *It can be true*) when you're talking about one particular thing.

intro: We use the **second conditional** to talk about **unreal or unlikely** situations in the present or future, and their results: *If I **had** a million dollars, I**'d buy** a house by the sea.* (I don't have a million dollars.)

rows: If I **lived** in the city, I **would walk** to work.
If I **spoke** Japanese, I **could** work in Tokyo.

blocks.md: *Would* is often contracted: *I**'d**, you**'d**, she**'d***. The past tense here doesn't mean past time. It shows that the situation is **unreal**.
Don't use *would* in the *if* clause: *If I **had** time…* (not *If I would have time*).

With *be*, you can use **were** for all persons: *If I **were** rich… If she **were** here…* (*was* is also common in everyday speech). ***If I were you**, I'd…* is a common way to give advice: *If I were you, I'd talk to her.*

rows: *If I **win** the match, I**'ll** be happy.* (I might win.)
*If I **won** the lottery, I**'d** stop working.* (It's very unlikely.)
*If I **were** taller, I'd play basketball.* (I'm not tall.)

blocks.md: See [Zero and First Conditional](/blog/grammar/zero-and-first-conditional/) and [Third Conditional](/blog/grammar/third-conditional/).

intro: We use the **third conditional** to imagine a different past: something that didn't happen, and what its result would have been. *If I **had left** earlier, I **would have caught** the train.* (I didn't leave earlier, so I missed the train.)
We often use it to talk about **regrets** and to **criticise**: *If you'd told me, I could have helped.*

sections.h2: How to form the third conditional

blocks.md: You can change the order of the clauses. Use a comma only when the if clause comes first: *If you had asked me, I would have helped.* / *I would have helped if you had asked me.*
In speech we use contractions: *If I**'d** known, I**'d have** told you.* The first **'d** = *had*; the second **'d** = *would*. *Would have* often sounds like *would've*, but never write *would of*.
Instead of *would have*, use **could have** for a possible ability and **might have** for a possible (not certain) result:

items.text: If you had told me, I **could have** helped.
items.note: = I would have been able to help

items.text: If it had stopped raining, we **might have** gone to the beach.
What **would** you **have done** if you **had lost** your passport?
**Would** you **have come** if I**'d invited** you?
If he **hadn't called**, I **wouldn't have known**.

rows: if + past simple, would + base verb
if + past perfect, would have + past participle
If I had more time, I would visit you.
If I had had more time, I would have visited you.

blocks.md: *Had had* is correct. The first *had* makes the past perfect; the second is the past participle of *have*.
More practice: [Second Conditional](/blog/grammar/second-conditional/) and [Zero and First Conditional](/blog/grammar/zero-and-first-conditional/).

topics.h1: Future Time Clauses (when, as soon as, until)
intro: After **when, as soon as, until, before, after** and **once**, we use the **present simple** (not *will*) to talk about the future: *I'll call you **when** I **get** home.* (not *when I will get home*)

rows: **As soon as** the film **ends**, we'll go.

blocks.md: The other clause uses a future form or an imperative: *I**'ll** call you when I arrive. **Text** me when you arrive.*

sections.h2: The present perfect to show completion

blocks.md: Use the **present perfect** to show that the first action will be finished before the second one happens: *I'll go to bed **when** I**'ve finished** this chapter. You can leave **as soon as** you**'ve done** the test.*

sections.h2: If and unless work the same way

blocks.md: *If it **rains**, we'll stay at home.* (not *If it will rain*) More practice: [Zero and First Conditional](/blog/grammar/zero-and-first-conditional/).
*When* = you're sure it will happen: *I'll call you **when** I get home.* *If* = it might happen: *I'll call you **if** I have time.*

intro: We use **reported speech** to say what someone said without repeating their exact words: *“I'm tired.” → She **said** (that) she **was** tired.*
After a past reporting verb (*said, told, asked*), the tense usually moves **one step back** into the past.

rows: past simple: *He said he **worked** at home.*
past perfect: *She said she **had seen** him.*
had to: *She said she **had to** go.*

blocks.md: The tense change is not always necessary. If something is still true, you can keep the tense: *“I live in Toronto.” → He said he **lives** (or **lived**) in Toronto.* In speech, people also often keep the past simple: *She said she **saw** him.*
If the reporting verb is in the present (*says, tells*), don't change the tense: *She **says** she**'s** tired.*

items: **say** + (that) + sentence: *He **said** (that) he was hungry.*
**tell** + person + (that) + sentence: *He **told me** (that) he was hungry.*

blocks.md: Don't use a person after *say* (not *He said me…*), and don't use *tell* without a person (not *He told that…*). Some fixed phrases are different: *tell the truth, tell a lie, tell a story.* *That* is optional after both verbs.
Change pronouns to match the new speaker: *“I love **your** idea,” Sam told me. → Sam told me **he** loved **my** idea.* When the time or place is different, the time and place words change too:

rows: the day before / the previous day
the next day / the following day
the week before / the previous week

blocks.md: Only change these words when the time or place has changed. If you report something on the same day, *today* can stay *today*.
Reported questions use **normal sentence word order** (subject + verb), no *do / does / did* and no question mark. Use **ask**, not *say*.

rows: *He asked **if I had seen** the match.*

blocks.md: For yes/no questions, use **if** or **whether**: *He asked **if** I was ready.*
Use **ask / tell + person + to + base verb**. For negatives, use **not to**: *“Please sit down.” → She **asked me to sit** down. “Don't touch it.” → He **told us not to touch** it.*

items.text: *“I'm busy.”* → She said she **was** busy.
*“I work in a hotel.”* → He told me he **worked** in a hotel.
*“We're leaving.”* → They said they **were leaving**.
*“I lost my wallet.”* → She said she **had lost** her wallet.
*“I've never been to Japan.”* → He said he **had** never **been** to Japan.
*“I'll help you.”* → She said she **would** help me.
*“I can't come tomorrow.”* → He said he **couldn't** come **the next day**.
items.note: can't → couldn't; tomorrow → the next day

items.text: *“Where is the station?”* → She asked me where the station **was**.
*“Do you like jazz?”* → He asked me **if** I **liked** jazz.
*“Please close the window.”* → She asked me **to close** the window.

topics.h1: The Passive: Present and Past Simple
intro: We use the **passive** when the action is more important than the person who does it, or when we don't know who did it: *Paper **is made** from wood. My bike **was stolen** last night.*
Form it with **be + past participle**: *is/are made* (present), *was/were made* (past).

rows: They make cars in this factory.
Someone cleans the office every day.

blocks.md: Only **be** changes: *is/are* for the present, *was/were* for the past. The past participle stays the same: *made, built, written, sent.* For irregular past participles, see the [irregular verbs list](/blog/grammar/past-simple/).

rows: Yes, it is. / No, it isn't.
Yes, it was. / No, it wasn't.

blocks.md: Passive questions and negatives use **be**, not *do* or *did*: *Was the house built in 1900?* (not *Did the house built…?*)

sections.h2: When do we use the passive?

items: We don't know who did it: *My phone **was stolen**.*
It's obvious or not important who does it: *The rubbish **is collected** on Mondays.*
The thing is more interesting than the person: *This song **was written** in 1971.*
News, science and processes: *Two people **were injured** in the accident. The water **is heated** to 100°C.*

sections.h2: By + the person who does the action

blocks.md: Use **by** to say who did the action, but only when this information is important or interesting: *The Mona Lisa **was painted by** Leonardo da Vinci.*
Don't add *by people*, *by someone* or *by them*: *English is spoken here* (not *English is spoken by people here*).
Both are correct grammar. Choose the one that starts with the thing you're talking about:

items.text: A dog **bit** my brother.
items.note: active: the sentence is about the dog

items.text: My brother **was bitten** by a dog.
items.note: passive: the sentence is about my brother

items.text: Coffee **is grown** in Brazil and Colombia.
Dinner **is served** from 7 to 10 pm.
items.note: present: who serves it isn't important

intro: A **defining relative clause** tells us **which** person or thing we mean. Without it, the sentence isn't clear: *The woman **who lives next door** is a doctor.*
We don't use commas around defining relative clauses.

rows: The man **who** called you is my uncle.
The bike **which** I bought was cheap.
people or things (very common in speech)
The man **that** called you… / The bike **that** I bought…
She's the girl **whose** brother is a pilot.
I remember the day **when** we met.

blocks.md: In American English, *that* is much more common than *which* in defining clauses. Both are correct.

sections.h2: When can you leave out who, which or that?

blocks.md: You can leave out the pronoun when it is the **object** of the clause, that is, when another subject comes after it: *The book (**that**) **I**'m reading is great.* You **can't** leave it out when it is the **subject**: *The man **who** lives next door…* (not *The man lives next door…*).

items.text: The film (that) we watched was boring.
The people who work here are friendly.

blocks.md: The relative pronoun replaces *he, she, it* or *them*, so don't add another pronoun: *The bike which I bought was cheap.* (not *The bike which I bought it…*)

*Where* = *in / at which*: *the hotel **where** we stayed* = *the hotel **that** we stayed **in***. In everyday English, prepositions usually go at the end: *the person (who) I spoke **to***. In formal English: *the person **to whom** I spoke*.
*Whose* replaces *his, her, its, their*: *I know a man. **His** car is electric.* → *I know a man **whose** car is electric.*

intro: A **question tag** is a short question at the end of a sentence. We use it to check information or to ask someone to agree: *It's cold today, **isn't it**? You don't eat meat, **do you**?*

items: Positive sentence → negative tag: *She's French, **isn't she**?*
Negative sentence → positive tag: *He can't swim, **can he**?*
Use the same auxiliary verb as the sentence (*be, have, can, will…*). If there is no auxiliary, use **do / does / did**: *You live here, **don't you**? She called you, **didn't she**?*
The tag uses a pronoun, not a noun: *Your brother works here, doesn't **he**?*
*I am* → **aren't I**: *I'm late, **aren't I**?*
*Let's* → **shall we**: *Let's go, **shall we**?*
Imperatives → **will you / can you / would you**: *Close the door, **will you**?*
*Never, nobody, nothing, hardly* make the sentence negative, so the tag is positive: *You **never** call me, **do** you?*
*There is / there are* → **isn't there / aren't there**: *There's a problem, **isn't there**?*
*Everyone, someone, nobody* → **they**: *Everyone's here, **aren't they**?*

blocks.md: Sometimes people use a positive tag after a positive sentence to show surprise or interest: *So you're moving to Spain, **are you**?* In the exercises below, choose the normal tag for checking information.
If your voice goes **down** at the end, you're fairly sure and you want the other person to agree. If your voice goes **up**, it's a real question and you aren't sure of the answer.

intro: A **gerund** is the -ing form of a verb used like a noun: ***Swimming** is good for you.* An **infinitive** is *to* + base verb: *I want **to swim**.*
After some verbs we use the gerund, and after others the infinitive. You need to learn which verbs go with which form.

blocks.md: *enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest, keep, practise (UK) / practice (US), consider, miss, imagine, can't stand, don't mind, give up*

items.text: I **enjoy cooking**.
She **avoided answering** the question.
**Would** you **mind closing** the door?

blocks.md: *want, decide, hope, plan, promise, agree, refuse, offer, learn, manage, need, seem, afford, would like*

items.text: We **decided to stay** at home.
He **refused to help** us.
I can't **afford to buy** a new car.

blocks.md: For a negative infinitive, put **not** before *to*: *He promised **not to be** late.*
*ask, tell, want, invite, encourage, allow, remind, advise* + person + **to**: *My parents **want me to study** law. She **reminded me to call** the bank.*
Not *want that…*: *I want **you to come**.* (not *I want that you come*)

sections.h2: -ing after prepositions and as a subject

items: After a preposition, always use -ing: *I'm interested **in learning** Japanese. Thanks **for helping** me. She left **without saying** goodbye.*
As the subject of a sentence: ***Learning** a language takes time.*

blocks.md: In *look forward to* and *be used to*, **to** is a preposition, so it takes -ing: *I'm looking forward **to seeing** you.*

*like, love, hate, prefer, start, begin, continue* can take either form with little or no change in meaning: *I like **swimming** / I like **to swim**. It started **raining** / It started **to rain**.* After *would like, would love, would prefer*, use **to**: *I'd like **to go**.*

A few verbs change their meaning: *I stopped **smoking*** (I don't smoke now) but *I stopped **to smoke*** (I stopped what I was doing in order to smoke). *Remember, forget* and *try* work in a similar way.

topics.h1: Quantifiers: All, Both, Either, Neither, None, Few
intro: **Quantifiers** say how many or how much: ***All** my friends came. **Neither** of us knew the answer. **None** of the shops were open.*
Some quantifiers talk about **two** things (*both, either, neither*) and some about **three or more** (*all, most, none*).

rows: one or the other (it doesn't matter which)
not one and not the other

blocks.md: *Either* and *neither* + **singular noun**: *neither answer*. With *of* + plural: *neither **of** the answers*. After *either of / neither of*, the verb is often singular in formal English and plural in speech: *Neither of them **is** / **are** ready.* Both are used.

sections.h2: Three or more: all, most, some, none

rows: **Most** people like chocolate. **Most of** my friends live here.

blocks.md: *None of* + plural noun can take a singular or a plural verb: *None of the shops **was** / **were** open.* Both are correct.
Directly before a noun, use **no**, not *none*: *There are **no** buses.* *None* is used alone or with *of*: *None of the buses… – How many buses? – **None**.*

Use *of* before *the, my, these* and other determiners, and before pronouns: ***Most of the** people… **All of them**… **Both of us**…* Without a determiner, don't use *of*: ***Most people** like music.* (not *Most of people*)
With *all* and *both*, *of* is optional before *the / my*: *all (of) the students, both (of) my sisters.* Before a pronoun you always need it: ***both of them**, **all of us**, **neither of you**.*

**Each** = every one, seen separately (two or more): *Each student has a book.* **Every** = all the members of a group of three or more: *Every room has a balcony.* Both take a **singular** noun and verb.

*A few* = some, a small number (positive). *Few* = not many, almost none (negative): *I have **a few** friends here, so I'm happy.* / *I have **few** friends here, so I'm lonely.* See also [Much, Many, A Lot Of, A Few, A Little](/blog/grammar/much-many-a-few-a-little/).

intro: We use **reflexive pronouns** (*myself, yourself, himself…*) when the subject and the object are the **same person**: *I cut **myself**.*
We use **each other** when two or more people do something **to the other person**: *Tom and Anna love **each other**.*

rows: He looked at **himself** in the mirror.

items: **Same person** as the subject: *She burned **herself** on the cooker. Enjoy **yourself**!*
**Emphasis** (that person and nobody else): *I painted the house **myself**. The president **himself** opened the hospital.*
**by + reflexive** = alone, without help: *He lives **by himself**. I did it **by myself**.*

sections.h2: Verbs that usually don't need a reflexive pronoun

blocks.md: In English, we don't usually use a reflexive pronoun with *relax, feel, concentrate, meet, get up, sit down*, and usually not with *wash, dress, shave*: *I **relaxed** on the sofa* (not *relaxed myself*). *I **feel** tired.* *He **got dressed** quickly.*
Use *wash / dress myself* only when it's a special effort: *My son is three, but he can already **dress himself**.*

*They looked at **themselves*** = each person looked at himself or herself (in a mirror). *They looked at **each other*** = A looked at B and B looked at A. *One another* means the same as *each other*.

topics.h1: Both, Either, Neither and Not Only
intro: We use **both, either** and **neither** to talk about **two** people or things: ***Both** my sisters live in Toronto. You can have **either** tea **or** coffee. **Neither** Tom **nor** Anna came.*
**Not only… but also** adds a second, often surprising, point: *She speaks **not only** English **but also** Chinese.*

rows: **Both** my brother **and** my sister are doctors.
We can go **either** by bus **or** by train.
**Neither** my phone **nor** my laptop is working.
The hotel was **not only** cheap **but also** comfortable.

blocks.md: With *neither… nor* and *either… or*, the verb usually agrees with the noun closest to it: *Neither my parents nor my **sister is** coming.*

sections.h2: Both of, either of, neither of

blocks.md: Before *the, my, these* or a pronoun, use **of**: ***Both of** my parents. **Either of** these days is fine. **Neither of** us likes coffee.*

items: *both* + plural verb: ***Both of** them **are** here.*
*either* + singular noun: ***Either day** is fine for me.*
*neither of* + plural noun: the verb can be singular (more formal) or plural (informal): *Neither of my friends **is / are** coming.*

blocks.md: *Neither* already has a negative meaning, so don't add *not*: *Neither of them came* (not *Neither of them didn't come*).

sections.h2: Too, either and neither in short answers

rows: *Me too.* / *So do I.* / *I love it too.*
*Me neither.* / *Neither do I.* / *I don't like them either.*

blocks.md: Use *too* in positive sentences and *either* in negative sentences: *I don't eat meat **either*** (not *too*).

topics.h1: Although, Despite and In Spite Of
intro: We use **although, despite** and **in spite of** to show contrast: something is true, but it's surprising because of something else. *We went out **although** it was raining. We went out **despite** the rain.*
The difference is grammar: what comes after each word.

rows: **Despite** the cold, we swam. **In spite of** feeling tired, she kept going.
**despite / in spite of + the fact that**
**Despite the fact that** it was cold, we swam.

blocks.md: Never say *despite of*. It's **despite** or **in spite of**.

*Though* is a little more informal than *although*. *Even though* is stronger: it shows more surprise. *Though* can also go at the end of a sentence, meaning *however*: *It was expensive. I bought it, **though**.*
*But* joins two clauses in one sentence: *It was raining, **but** we went out.* *However* usually starts a new sentence: *It was raining. **However**, we went out.*
Don't use *although* and *but* in the same sentence: ***Although** it was late, we stayed.* (not *Although it was late, but we stayed*)

items.text: **Although** she was tired, she finished her work.
**Despite** the traffic, we arrived on time.
**In spite of** the bad weather, the match went ahead.
He went to work **even though** he was ill.
**Despite** having little money, they were happy.
I enjoyed the film, **though** it was a bit long.
**Despite the fact that** he trained hard, he lost the race.
**In spite of** losing the first game, they won the tournament.
The restaurant was expensive. The food was great, **though**.
It was sunny. **However**, it was quite cold.

mistakes.wrong: Despite it was raining, we went out.
mistakes.right: Although it was raining, we went out.
mistakes.why: Despite isn't followed by a clause. (Or: Despite the rain, we went out.)

mistakes.wrong: Although the rain, we went out.
mistakes.right: Despite the rain, we went out.
mistakes.why: Although needs a clause; use despite before a noun.

mistakes.wrong: In spite the noise, I slept well.
mistakes.right: In spite of the noise, I slept well.
mistakes.why: In spite of — don't forget of.

mistakes.wrong: Despite of the cost, they bought it.
mistakes.right: Despite the cost, they bought it.
mistakes.why: There is no despite of.

mistakes.wrong: Although it was late, but we stayed.
mistakes.right: Although it was late, we stayed.
mistakes.why: Don't use although and but together.

mistakes.wrong: Despite he was tired, he drove home.
mistakes.right: Despite being tired, he drove home.
mistakes.why: Despite + -ing (or although + clause).

topics.h1: Modifying Comparatives (much better, twice as big)
intro: We can say **how much** bigger, better or more expensive something is by putting a word before the comparative: *much bigger, slightly cheaper, far better, even worse.*
We can also modify **as… as**: *just as good as, twice as expensive as, nowhere near as fast as.*

rows: The train is **much faster** than the bus.
The first film was good, but this one is **even better**.

blocks.md: Don't use *very* with comparatives: *much better* (not *very better*). And don't use *more* with -er: *much faster* (not *more faster*).
The same words work with *more* + adjective: *a lot **more** expensive, slightly **more** comfortable, far **less** interesting.*

items: the same: ***just as** good **as**, **exactly as** big **as***
almost the same: ***nearly as** fast **as**, **almost as** tall **as***
not quite the same: *not **quite as** warm **as***
a big difference: *not **nearly as** / **nowhere near as** expensive **as***
multiples: ***twice as** big **as**, **three times as** expensive **as***

blocks.md: Repeat the comparative for something that keeps changing: *It's getting **harder and harder**. Prices are going up **more and more** quickly.*
Use ***the** + comparative, **the** + comparative* when one change causes another: ***The more** you practise, **the better** you get. **The sooner**, **the better**.*

items.text: My new job is **much more interesting** than my old one.
Could you speak **a bit more slowly**, please?
The test was **far easier** than I expected.
It's cold today, but tomorrow will be **even colder**.
Their house is **twice as big as** ours.
The sequel isn't **nearly as good as** the first film.
Online tickets are **just as expensive as** tickets at the station.
The weather isn't **quite as warm as** yesterday.
English is becoming **more and more** important.
**The older** I get, **the less** I worry.

mistakes.why: Use much, far or a lot with comparatives, not very.

intro: Many verbs are followed by a **fixed preposition** before their object: *It **depends on** the weather. This bag **belongs to** me. I'm **waiting for** the bus.*
After the preposition, use a noun, a pronoun or verb**-ing**: *She apologised **for being** late.*

belong to, listen to, talk to, apologise to, happen to
wait for, look for, pay for, apologise for, ask for
Can I **pay for** this by card?

blocks.md: *Arrive **in*** a city or country, *arrive **at*** a building or place: *We arrived in Rome. We arrived at the hotel.* Never *arrive to*.

Some verbs take a direct object with **no preposition**, even though your language may use one: *discuss **the plan*** (not *discuss about*), *marry **someone*** (not *marry with*), *enter **the room***, *call / phone **someone***, *reach **the top***, *answer **the question***.

items: *look **at*** (with your eyes), *look **for*** (try to find), *look **after*** (take care of)
*think **about*** (consider), *think **of*** (have an idea or opinion): *What do you think of my new hat?*
*agree **with*** a person, *agree **to*** a plan or request: *They agreed to our offer.*

topics.summary: One step further back in the past: When I arrived, the film had started.
intro: We use the **past perfect** (*had* + past participle) for something that happened **before** another moment in the past: *When I arrived, the film **had** already **started**.*
It takes you one step further back than the past simple. If you need to review the past simple first, see [Past Simple](/blog/grammar/past-simple/).

points.title: Form and main use: something earlier in the past
points.summary: had + past participle for an action before another past moment.

rows: Had she called? – No, she hadn't.

blocks.md: *Had* is the same for every person: *I had, you had, she had, they had.* Use the **past participle**: *gone, eaten, seen, been* (not *went, ate, saw*). See the list of irregular verbs on [Past Simple](/blog/grammar/past-simple/).
Think of two past moments. The past perfect is the **earlier** one: *I couldn't get in* (past) *because I **had lost** my keys* (earlier).
In speech, *had* is often **'d**: *I'd forgotten. They'd gone.* Be careful: *'d* can also mean *would* (*I'd like*). If a past participle follows, it's *had*.

examples.text: I couldn't get in because I **had lost** my keys.
She was tired because she **had worked** all night.
I **hadn't seen** the film, so I didn't know the ending.
**Had** you **been** to Asia before that trip?
The streets were wet. It**'d rained** in the night.

mistakes.wrong: I had went to bed early.
mistakes.right: I had gone to bed early.
mistakes.why: Use the past participle: gone.

mistakes.wrong: Had you ate before you came?
mistakes.right: Had you eaten before you came?
mistakes.why: Use the past participle: eaten.

mistakes.wrong: She was tired because she had work all day.
mistakes.right: She was tired because she had worked all day.
mistakes.why: had + past participle (worked).

points.title: Past simple or past perfect? The order of events
points.summary: Past simple for events in order; past perfect for an event that happened earlier than the one you're talking about.

blocks.md: The tense changes the **order** of events:

items: *When I arrived, the film **started**.* = I arrived, then the film started.
*When I arrived, the film **had started**.* = The film started first, then I arrived.

blocks.md: When you tell events **in the order they happened**, use the past simple. Don't use the past perfect for every past action: *I **woke up**, **had** a shower and **left** the house.*

examples.text: When we got to the station, the train **had left**.
When we got to the station, the train **left**.
When I got home, someone **had eaten** my cake.
I **got up**, **made** breakfast and **went** for a run.
I didn't know the way because I **hadn't been** there before.

mistakes.wrong: I had woken up, had had breakfast and had left.
mistakes.right: I woke up, had breakfast and left.
mistakes.why: Events in order: past simple.

mistakes.wrong: When I arrived, the film has started.
mistakes.right: When I arrived, the film had started.
mistakes.why: Earlier than a past moment: past perfect.

points.title: By the time, already, just, never … before
points.summary: by the time + past simple, then past perfect; already, just, never … before with the past perfect.

rows: *By the time we arrived, the concert **had finished**.*
*He **had just sat** down when the phone rang.*
*When she moved to Canada, she **had never seen** snow.*
***Had** you **ever** tried sushi before that night?*

blocks.md: *Already, just, never* and *ever* go between *had* and the past participle: *had **already** left, had **just** sat, had **never** seen.*

examples.text: By the time we got there, everyone **had gone** home.
She **had already ordered** when I arrived.
I**'d just got** into bed when the alarm went off.
He was nervous because he **had never flown** before.
By the time I finished my degree, my parents **had moved** to Canada.

mistakes.wrong: By the time we got there, the shop closed.
mistakes.right: By the time we got there, the shop had closed.
mistakes.why: By the time + earlier event: past perfect.

mistakes.wrong: She had left already when I called.
mistakes.right: She had already left when I called.
mistakes.why: Already goes between had and the participle.

points.title: Present perfect or past perfect?
points.summary: have done = before now; had done = before a moment in the past.

rows: *Until I moved to Canada, I**'d** never **seen** snow.*

blocks.md: The present perfect connects the past to **now**. The past perfect connects an earlier past to **a moment in the past**.

examples.text: I can't come out. I **haven't finished** my homework.
I couldn't go out because I **hadn't finished** my homework.
Last summer I visited Rome. I**'d** never **been** there before.
When I met him, he **had been** in the army for ten years.

mistakes.wrong: Before I came to Canada, I have never seen snow.
mistakes.right: Before I came to Canada, I had never seen snow.
mistakes.why: Before a past moment: past perfect.

mistakes.wrong: I'm not hungry. I'd already eaten.
mistakes.right: I'm not hungry. I've already eaten.
mistakes.why: Connected to now: present perfect.

points.title: It was the first time I'd…; states up to a past moment
points.summary: It was the first time / the best … I'd ever + past perfect; state verbs up to a past moment use the past perfect simple.

blocks.md: After *It was the first / second / third time…* and after superlatives (*the best, the worst…*) in the past, use the past perfect: *It was the first time I**'d been** on a plane. It was the best meal we**'d** ever **had**.*

To say **how long** a state continued up to a past moment, use the past perfect simple with state verbs: *They **had known** each other for years when they got married.* (not *had been knowing*). For actions, the past perfect continuous is common: *She **had been working** there for ten years when she left.*

examples.text: It was the first time she**'d been** on a plane.
That was the third time he**'d lost** his phone that month.
It was the most beautiful place I**'d** ever **seen**.
We **had known** each other for years before we started working together.
I**'d had** the car for only a month when it broke down.

mistakes.wrong: It was the first time I've been abroad.
mistakes.right: It was the first time I'd been abroad.
mistakes.why: It was the first time + past perfect.

mistakes.wrong: We had been knowing each other for ten years.
mistakes.right: We had known each other for ten years.
mistakes.why: Know is a state: past perfect simple.

points.title: When the past perfect is optional
points.summary: If the order is already clear (after, as soon as, before) the past simple is also fine; once the earlier time is set, you can continue in the past simple.

blocks.md: When a time word like *after, as soon as* or *before* already makes the order clear, the past simple is also correct and the meaning doesn't change: *After she **had finished** / **finished** work, she went home.*

When you have **set up** an earlier time with the past perfect, you don't have to keep using it. You can continue in the past simple: *I sold my old guitar last week. I**'d had** it since I was fifteen, and I **played** it almost every day.*

But keep the past perfect when the past simple would change the order: *When I got home, my son **had cooked** dinner* (it was ready) vs *When I got home, my son **cooked** dinner* (he started after I arrived).

examples.text: After the guests **had gone** / **went**, we cleaned up.
As soon as I**'d sent** / **sent** the message, I regretted it.
She asked about the salary before she **accepted** the job.
We**'d lived** in that flat for years. We **loved** it, but it was too small.
When the police arrived, the thief **had escaped**.

mistakes.wrong: After we have eaten, we went for a walk.
mistakes.right: After we had eaten (or After we ate), we went for a walk.
mistakes.why: A past sequence: past perfect or past simple, not present perfect.

points.title: Past perfect in reported speech and thoughts
points.summary: A present perfect becomes past perfect when reported in the past; a past simple can become past perfect or stay the same.

blocks.md: When we report words or thoughts in the past, a **present perfect** usually becomes **past perfect**: *'I've met him before.' → I was sure I**'d met** him before.*
A **past simple** can become past perfect, but it can also stay in the past simple, especially when the time is clear: *'I lost my keys.' → She said she **had lost** / **lost** her keys.*
If the situation is still true now, you can also keep the present perfect: *He told me he**'s** never **been** to Asia.* See [Reported Speech](/blog/grammar/reported-speech/).

examples.text: 'I've finished.' → She said she **had finished**.
'We haven't decided yet.' → They said they **hadn't decided** yet.
'I lost my phone.' → He said he **had lost** / **lost** his phone.
I realised I**'d left** my umbrella on the bus.
Police said twenty people **had been** / **were** injured.

mistakes.wrong: I was sure that I have met him before.
mistakes.right: I was sure that I had met him before.
mistakes.why: Reported in the past: present perfect → past perfect.

mistakes.wrong: She said she hasn't finish yet.
mistakes.right: She said she hadn't finished yet.
mistakes.why: Past perfect, with the past participle finished.

points.title: Plans that didn't happen: I had hoped to…
points.summary: had hoped / meant / intended / planned / wanted to = a plan or wish that didn't happen.

blocks.md: Use *had* + *hoped, meant, intended, planned, wanted, expected* + to-infinitive for a plan or wish that **didn't happen**: *I **had hoped** to finish by Friday, but my computer broke.*

The past simple and the continuous forms are also used with a similar meaning: *I **hoped** / **was hoping** / **had been hoping** to see you.* The past perfect makes it clearest that it didn't happen.

examples.text: We**'d hoped** to visit the museum, but it was closed.
I**'d meant** to call you, but I forgot.
She **had intended** to stay a week, but she left after two days.
They **had planned** to retire at 60, but they're still working.
I **was hoping** to see you at the party.

mistakes.wrong: I had hope to finish today, but I couldn't.
mistakes.right: I had hoped to finish today, but I couldn't.
mistakes.why: had + past participle: hoped.

mistakes.wrong: We had wanted visit you.
mistakes.right: We had wanted to visit you.
mistakes.why: had wanted + to-infinitive.

topics.summary: Now, around now, plans and changes: I'm working, are you coming?
intro: We use the **present continuous** for actions happening **now** or **around now**: *I**'m reading** a book. She**'s studying** for her exams this week.*
Form it with **am / is / are + verb-ing**. At higher levels it is also used for future plans, changing situations and annoying habits.

points.title: Form and use: I'm working (now)
points.summary: am / is / are + verb-ing for something happening at the moment of speaking.

rows: I**'m working**. He**'s sleeping**. They**'re playing**.
I**'m not working**. She **isn't sleeping**. We **aren't playing**.
Yes, + subject + am / is / are. / No, + subject + 'm not / isn't / aren't.
Yes, I am. / No, she isn't.
question word + **am / is / are** + subject + verb-ing?
work → working, read → reading, play → playing
Verb ends in **-e**: drop the e
make → making, write → writing, come → coming
One vowel + one consonant at the end of a stressed syllable: double the consonant
run → running, sit → sitting, swim → swimming, stop → stopping
Verb ends in **-ie**: change ie to **-ying**
lie → lying, die → dying, tie → tying

blocks.md: Use it for something happening **at the moment of speaking**. Common words: *now, right now, at the moment, Look!, Listen!*

In speaking we usually use contractions: *I'm, you're, he's, she's, it's, we're, they're.* British and American spelling differ for some verbs ending in -l: *travelling* (UK) / *traveling* (US). Both are correct.

examples.text: I**'m cooking** dinner right now.
She **isn't working** today.
**Are** you **listening** to me?
Look! It**'s snowing**!
He**'s sitting** next to the window.

mistakes.wrong: I working now.
mistakes.right: I'm working now.
mistakes.why: Don't forget am / is / are.

mistakes.wrong: She is work at the moment.
mistakes.right: She is working at the moment.
mistakes.why: Use verb-ing.

mistakes.wrong: He is runing.
mistakes.right: He is running.
mistakes.why: Run → running (double the n).

mistakes.wrong: What you are doing?
mistakes.right: What are you doing?
mistakes.why: Question order: are + subject + verb-ing.

points.title: Around now and temporary situations
points.summary: Use the present continuous for things happening around now (this week, at the moment) and temporary situations.

blocks.md: The action can be happening **around now**, not exactly at this second: *I**'m reading** a great book at the moment.* (Maybe I'm not reading it right now, but I've started and haven't finished.)
It's also used for **temporary** situations: *My cousin **is staying** with us this month. Sam **is working** from home this week.*
Common words: *at the moment, today, this week, this month, this year, currently.*

examples.text: I**'m reading** a great book at the moment.
My cousin **is staying** with us this month.
We**'re learning** about volcanoes in class this week.
Ben **is learning** Japanese this year.
How **is** your new job **going**?

mistakes.wrong: I read a really good book at the moment.
mistakes.right: I'm reading a really good book at the moment.
mistakes.why: Around now: present continuous.

mistakes.wrong: My sister stays with us this month.
mistakes.right: My sister is staying with us this month.
mistakes.why: A temporary situation: present continuous.

points.title: Future arrangements: I'm meeting Sam tonight
points.summary: Use the present continuous for future plans that are already arranged, usually with a time.

blocks.md: Use the present continuous for **future arrangements**: plans you've already made, often with a time, a place or other people: *I**'m meeting** Sam at 6 tonight. We**'re flying** to Rome on Monday.*
Common words: *tonight, tomorrow, on Friday, next week, at the weekend.*
*Be going to* is also correct for plans: *I'm going to meet Sam at 6.* For timetables, use the present simple: *The film **starts** at 8.* See [Future Forms](/blog/grammar/future-forms/).

examples.text: I**'m meeting** Sam at 6 tonight.
We**'re flying** to Rome on Monday.
What **are** you **doing** this weekend?
She**'s starting** her new job next week.
They **aren't coming** to the party.

mistakes.wrong: I see the dentist tomorrow. (my appointment)
mistakes.right: I'm seeing the dentist tomorrow.
mistakes.why: Personal arrangements: present continuous.

mistakes.wrong: What do you do this weekend?
mistakes.right: What are you doing this weekend?
mistakes.why: Asking about plans: present continuous.

points.title: Changing situations: It's getting colder
points.summary: Use the present continuous for situations that are changing now: get, become, increase, improve.

blocks.md: Use the present continuous for a **change that is happening** at the moment: *The weather **is getting** colder. Prices **are rising**.*
Verbs often used this way: *get, become, change, improve, increase, rise, fall, grow, start, begin.* *Get* + comparative is very common: *It's **getting darker**. Your English is **getting better**.*

examples.text: The weather **is getting** colder.
Prices **are rising** again.
Your English **is improving** fast.
The city **is growing** every year.
I**'m starting** to enjoy my new job.

mistakes.wrong: The population increases very fast at the moment.
mistakes.right: The population is increasing very fast at the moment.
mistakes.why: A change happening now: present continuous.

mistakes.wrong: It gets dark. Let's go home.
mistakes.right: It's getting dark. Let's go home.
mistakes.why: A change happening now: present continuous.

points.title: always + continuous: He's always complaining
points.summary: always / constantly / forever + continuous for something that happens too often, often annoying.

blocks.md: *Always, constantly* or *forever* + present continuous means something happens **very often, often too often**. We usually use it to complain: *He**'s always complaining**. You**'re forever losing** your keys!*
Compare: *I **always walk** to work* = every time, a normal habit (neutral).
Word order: **be + always + verb-ing**: *She**'s always interrupting** me.* (not *always is interrupting*)

examples.text: He**'s always complaining** about something.
You**'re always losing** your keys!
My neighbour **is constantly playing** loud music.
She**'s forever borrowing** my phone.
I **always walk** to work.

mistakes.wrong: She always is interrupting me.
mistakes.right: She's always interrupting me.
mistakes.why: Word order: be + always + verb-ing.

mistakes.wrong: I'm always going to work by bike. (my normal habit)
mistakes.right: I always go to work by bike.
mistakes.why: For a neutral habit, use the present simple.

points.title: In progress at a regular time; always for typical behaviour
points.summary: At 8 I'm usually driving = in the middle of it at that time; always + continuous can also describe typical (even positive) behaviour.

blocks.md: Use the present continuous for an action that is **in progress at a regular time**: *At 7 a.m. I**'m usually having** breakfast, so call me later.* Compare: *I usually **have** breakfast at 7* = that's when I start it.
*Always / constantly* + continuous describes **typical behaviour**. It's often a complaint, but it can also be positive: *My neighbour **is always bringing** us cakes. She's so kind.*

examples.text: At 7 a.m. I**'m usually having** breakfast.
Don't call between 6 and 7: we**'re usually eating** then.
On Saturday mornings I**'m normally working** in the garden.
She**'s always helping** other people.
Whenever I visit, he**'s watching** TV.

mistakes.wrong: At 8 I'm usually drive to work.
mistakes.right: At 8 I'm usually driving to work.
mistakes.why: be + verb-ing.

mistakes.wrong: She's always help people.
mistakes.right: She's always helping people.
mistakes.why: be + always + verb-ing.

points.title: When not to use it for the future
points.summary: Use the present continuous for arranged or decided plans, not for predictions or permanent future situations.

blocks.md: The present continuous for the future suggests something **arranged or firmly decided**: *I**'m not lending** him my car again.* So we don't use it for:

items: **Predictions** about things nobody can arrange, like the weather: *It**'s going to rain** tonight. / It**'ll rain** tonight.* (not *It's raining tonight*)
**Permanent** future situations: *People **will live** longer in the future.* (not *are living longer in the future*)

blocks.md: With **go** and **come**, many people prefer the present continuous to *going to go / going to come*: *I**'m going** to town on Saturday. **Are** you **coming** home for lunch?*

examples.text: I**'m going** to Toronto next week.
**Are** you **coming** home for lunch?
It**'s going to snow** tonight.
Experts say the population **will grow**.
I**'m not lending** him my car again.

mistakes.wrong: It's raining tomorrow.
mistakes.right: It's going to rain tomorrow. / It'll rain tomorrow.
mistakes.why: The weather can't be arranged: use going to or will.

mistakes.wrong: In the future, people are living on other planets.
mistakes.right: In the future, people will live on other planets.
mistakes.why: Predictions about the future: will or going to.

topics.summary: How to choose: I work (in general) or I'm working (now)?
intro: The **present simple** is for things **in general**: habits, facts and permanent situations. The **present continuous** is for things happening **now or around now**, and for **temporary** situations.
*I **work** from home on Fridays. I**'m working** from home today.*

points.title: Now or in general?
points.summary: Present continuous for now; present simple for habits, facts and things in general.

rows: every day, usually, often, never, on Mondays
now, right now, at the moment, Look!, Listen!

blocks.md: Some verbs (*know, want, like, understand…*) are not normally used in the continuous, even for now: *I **know** the answer* (not *I'm knowing*). See [Stative Verbs](/blog/grammar/stative-verbs/).

examples.text: I usually **walk** to work, but today I**'m taking** the bus.
Water **boils** at 100°C. Look, the water **is boiling**!
**Do** you **play** tennis? – Yes, but I**'m not playing** this week.
Where's Tom? – He**'s having** a shower.
My dad **cooks** on Sundays. He**'s cooking** right now.

mistakes.wrong: Look! The bus comes.
mistakes.right: Look! The bus is coming.
mistakes.why: Happening now: present continuous.

mistakes.wrong: I'm going to the gym every day.
mistakes.right: I go to the gym every day.
mistakes.why: A habit: present simple.

mistakes.wrong: She is speaking three languages.
mistakes.right: She speaks three languages.
mistakes.why: A permanent ability, not now: present simple.

points.title: Temporary or permanent?
points.summary: Present continuous for temporary situations; present simple for permanent ones.

rows: *I**'m living** with friends until I find a flat.*
*The river **is flowing** very fast today because of the rain.*

blocks.md: Words like *today, this week, this year, at the moment, until…* often show that a situation is temporary.

examples.text: I **work** in a bank, but this month I**'m working** in our Paris office.
We **live** in Ottawa. We**'re staying** with my aunt in Toronto this week.
Our company **isn't doing** very well this year.
He **teaches** maths, but this term he**'s teaching** physics too.

mistakes.wrong: I stay with my aunt until my flat is ready.
mistakes.right: I'm staying with my aunt until my flat is ready.
mistakes.why: A temporary situation: present continuous.

mistakes.wrong: My parents are living in the same house all their lives.
mistakes.right: My parents have lived in the same house all their lives.
mistakes.why: From the past until now: present perfect. See Present Perfect.

points.title: Stories, jokes and live commentary
points.summary: In informal stories and live commentary, the present continuous gives the background and the present simple gives the main events.

blocks.md: In **informal stories and jokes**, speakers often use present tenses to make the story more vivid. The **present continuous** gives the background; the **present simple** gives the main events, in order: *So I**'m standing** at the bus stop, and this man **comes** up to me and **asks** for my phone.*
After past tenses, a present simple verb can highlight a sudden event, often with *suddenly* or *all of a sudden*: *We were having dinner when all of a sudden the lights **go** out.*

**Live commentary** (sport, demonstrations) works the same way: present simple for quick, complete actions, present continuous for longer ones: *Silva **passes** to Jones… Jones **shoots**! The fans **are going** wild.*

examples.text: So I**'m waiting** for a taxi when a woman **runs** up to me…
A man **walks** into a café and **orders** a coffee…
It**'s raining**, it**'s getting** dark, and suddenly the car **stops**.
And she **serves**… it's an ace!
The crowd **is cheering** as the runners **cross** the line.

mistakes.wrong: So I'm walking home and suddenly a dog is jumping at me.
mistakes.right: So I'm walking home and suddenly a dog jumps at me.
mistakes.why: Main events: present simple.

mistakes.wrong: So I stand at the bus stop, and a man is coming up to me.
mistakes.right: So I'm standing at the bus stop, and a man comes up to me.
mistakes.why: Background: continuous; main event: simple.

items.prompt: My parents ___ in Toronto. They moved there in 1995.

topics.summary: Habits, facts, timetables and more: I work, she works, do you work?
intro: We use the **present simple** for habits, routines and things that are generally true: *I **drink** coffee every morning. The sun **rises** in the east.*
With **he, she, it**, add **-s** to the verb: *She **works** in a bank.* For negatives and questions, use **do / does**: *I **don't** like fish. **Does** he **speak** French?*

points.title: Form: I work, she works
points.summary: Use the base verb with I, you, we, they; add -s or -es with he, she, it.

rows: work → works, read → reads, live → lives
kiss → kisses, wash → washes, watch → watches, fix → fixes, go → goes, do → does
study → studies, try → tries, fly → flies
play → plays, buy → buys, enjoy → enjoys

blocks.md: **Be** is different: *I **am**, you **are**, she **is**.* Don't use *am / is / are* with another verb in the present simple: *I **work*** (not *I am work*).

examples.text: I **live** in a small flat.
My brother **works** in a hospital.
He **watches** football every weekend.
My daughter **studies** in the evening.
She **has** two cats.

mistakes.wrong: She work in a bank.
mistakes.right: She works in a bank.
mistakes.why: He / she / it: add -s.

mistakes.wrong: My mother haves two cars.
mistakes.right: My mother has two cars.
mistakes.why: Have → has.

mistakes.wrong: He watchs TV every night.
mistakes.right: He watches TV every night.
mistakes.why: Verbs ending in -ch add -es.

mistakes.wrong: I am work every day.
mistakes.right: I work every day.
mistakes.why: Don't add am / is / are.

points.title: Negatives and questions: don't, doesn't, do, does
points.summary: Negatives: don't / doesn't + base verb. Questions: do / does + subject + base verb.

blocks.md: Use **-s** only once. After *doesn't* and *does*, use the base verb: *She doesn't **work**. Does she **work**?* (not *doesn't works*)
Keep the question order: question word + *do / does* + subject + verb: *What **does** this word **mean**?* (not *What means this word?*)

examples.text: We **don't watch** TV in the morning.
She **doesn't eat** meat.
**Do** you **like** coffee? – Yes, I **do**.
**Does** your sister **speak** English?
What time **does** the shop **open**?

mistakes.wrong: He don't like coffee.
mistakes.right: He doesn't like coffee.
mistakes.why: He / she / it: doesn't.

mistakes.wrong: She doesn't works on Sundays.
mistakes.right: She doesn't work on Sundays.
mistakes.why: After doesn't, use the base verb.

mistakes.wrong: Does he plays tennis?
mistakes.right: Does he play tennis?
mistakes.why: After does, use the base verb.

mistakes.wrong: Where you live?
mistakes.right: Where do you live?
mistakes.why: Questions need do / does.

points.title: Uses: habits, facts and permanent situations
points.summary: Use the present simple for habits, routines, facts, permanent situations and likes.

items: Habits and routines: *I **get up** at 7 o'clock. We **play** football on Saturdays.*
Facts and things that are always true: *Water **boils** at 100°C. The sun **rises** in the east.*
Permanent situations: *My parents **live** in Toronto. She **works** for a big company.*
Likes, dislikes and opinions: *I **love** pizza. He **doesn't like** cold weather.*

blocks.md: Common time words: *every day, every week, on Mondays, in the morning, twice a week.* Ask about frequency with ***How often**…?*: *How often **do** you **go** to the gym?*

*Always, usually, often, sometimes, never* go **before** the main verb but **after** *be*: *I **usually** walk to work. He**'s always** late.* See [Adverbs of Frequency](/blog/grammar/adverbs-of-frequency/).

examples.text: I **get up** at 7 every day.
Water **boils** at 100°C.
My parents **live** in Toronto.
I **love** pizza, but I **don't like** pasta.
How often **do** you **go** to the gym? – Twice a week.

mistakes.wrong: She always is late.
mistakes.right: She is always late.
mistakes.why: Adverbs of frequency go after be.

mistakes.wrong: I go every day to work.
mistakes.right: I go to work every day.
mistakes.why: Time words like every day usually go at the end.

mistakes.wrong: Water is boiling at 100°C.
mistakes.right: Water boils at 100°C.
mistakes.why: For facts that are always true, use the present simple.

points.title: Timetables and schedules: The train leaves at 8
points.summary: Use the present simple for future events on a timetable or schedule.

blocks.md: Use the present simple for **future** events that are on a timetable or a fixed schedule: transport, films, classes, opening times. *The train **leaves** at 8:30 tomorrow. What time **does** the film **start** tonight?*

For **your own plans** with other people, use the present continuous or *be going to*, not the present simple: *I**'m meeting** Sam tonight.* (not *I meet Sam tonight*). See [Future Forms](/blog/grammar/future-forms/).

After *when, as soon as, before, after, until*, use the present simple for the future: *I'll call you when I **get** home.* (not *when I will get*). See [Future Time Clauses](/blog/grammar/future-time-clauses/).

examples.text: The train **leaves** at 8:30 tomorrow.
What time **does** the film **start** tonight?
My English course **starts** on Monday.
The museum **opens** at 10 on Sundays.
I'll text you when the plane **lands**.

mistakes.wrong: I meet my friends tonight. (my plan)
mistakes.right: I'm meeting my friends tonight.
mistakes.why: Personal arrangements: present continuous.

mistakes.wrong: I'll call you when I will get home.
mistakes.right: I'll call you when I get home.
mistakes.why: After when, use the present simple for the future.

points.title: I promise, I agree, I apologise: saying is doing
points.summary: Verbs like promise, agree and apologise do the action when you say them: use the present simple.

blocks.md: Some verbs **perform an action** when you say them. When you say *I promise*, you make a promise. With these verbs, use the present simple, not the continuous: *I **promise** I won't be late.* (not *I'm promising*)
Common verbs: *promise, agree, apologise, suggest, advise, insist, admit, refuse, warn, thank, congratulate, request.*
To sound more polite or formal, add a modal: *I **would suggest** leaving early. I **must insist** that you stay. We **would advise** you to book in advance.*

examples.text: I **promise** I'll call you tomorrow.
I **agree** with you.
I **apologise** for the delay.
I **suggest** we take a taxi.
I **would advise** you to book early.

mistakes.wrong: I'm promising I'll be careful.
mistakes.right: I promise I'll be careful.
mistakes.why: Saying it is the action: present simple.

mistakes.wrong: I'm agree with you.
mistakes.right: I agree with you.
mistakes.why: Agree is a verb: don't add am.

mistakes.wrong: I am apologising for the mistake.
mistakes.right: I apologise for the mistake.
mistakes.why: Saying it is the action: present simple.

points.title: Headlines, summaries, instructions and I hear
points.summary: The present simple is also used in headlines, plot summaries, instructions and to pass on news (I hear, I gather).

items: **Headlines** use the present simple for recent events: *Floods **hit** northern Italy. Minister **resigns**.*
**Summaries** of books, films and plays: *In the film, a young doctor **moves** to a small town and **discovers** a secret.*
**Instructions and demonstrations**: *First you **heat** the oil, then you **add** the onions.*
**Passing on news** with *I hear, I gather, I understand, they say, (someone) tells me*: *I **hear** you're moving to Vancouver. Anna **tells** me you've got a new job.*

blocks.md: In these uses, the present simple doesn't mean *now* or *regularly*. It's a convention that makes the text short and lively. In a summary, stay in the present simple: don't switch to the past in the middle.

examples.text: Scientists **discover** water on Mars.
In chapter 3, the author **compares** the two cities.
First you **mix** the flour and the eggs.
I **gather** the meeting has been cancelled.
My doctor **tells** me I need more exercise.

mistakes.wrong: In the film, the hero moves to London and was finding a job.
mistakes.right: In the film, the hero moves to London and finds a job.
mistakes.why: In a summary, keep the present simple.

mistakes.wrong: Anna is telling me you're engaged.
mistakes.right: Anna tells me you're engaged.
mistakes.why: To pass on news, use tells me.

items.prompt: I ___ I won't tell anyone.
items.explanation: Saying it makes the promise: present simple, *I promise*.

items.prompt: I ___ with you. It's a great idea.
items.explanation: *Agree* is a verb, used in the present simple: *I agree*.

items.prompt: I ___ for being late. It won't happen again.
items.explanation: Saying it is the apology: present simple, *I apologise*.

topics.summary: Verbs for states, not actions: I know (not I'm knowing), and when the continuous is possible.
intro: **Stative verbs** (state verbs) describe states, not actions: thoughts, feelings, senses, possession and existence.
We don't normally use them in continuous tenses: *I **know** the answer.* (not *I'm knowing*) *She **wants** a new phone.* (not *She's wanting*)

points.title: Verbs we don't use in the continuous
points.summary: know, want, like, need, understand, believe, belong… use the simple form, even for now.

rows: know, believe, understand, remember, forget, mean, realise, recognise
like, love, hate, prefer, want, need

blocks.md: Use the simple form **even when you mean now**: *I'm hungry. I **want** something to eat.* (not *I'm wanting*) *Do you **understand** what I mean?*
*Have* for possession is a state: *I **have** a car.* But *have* in phrases like *have lunch, have a shower, have fun* is an action, so the continuous is fine: *We**'re having** lunch.*

examples.text: I **don't understand** this question.
This bag **belongs** to my sister.
Do you **remember** her name?
How much **does** this jacket **cost**?
We**'re having** dinner at the moment.

mistakes.wrong: I'm knowing the answer.
mistakes.right: I know the answer.
mistakes.why: Know is a stative verb.

mistakes.wrong: This book is belonging to me.
mistakes.right: This book belongs to me.
mistakes.why: Belong is a stative verb.

mistakes.wrong: I'm having a car.
mistakes.right: I have a car.
mistakes.why: Have = own: a state.

points.title: Verbs with two meanings: think, have, see, taste
points.summary: Some verbs are states with one meaning and actions with another; only the action meaning can be continuous.

rows: *She**'s having** lunch / a shower / a good time.*

blocks.md: With *feel* (= how your body or mood is), both forms are fine: *I **feel** tired. / I**'m feeling** tired.* But *feel* = think is a state: *I **feel** you're right.*

examples.text: I**'m thinking** of moving to Montreal.
What **do** you **think** of my new haircut?
We**'re having** a great time.
This coffee **tastes** a bit strange.
Look! The cat **is looking** at the bird.

mistakes.wrong: I'm thinking this is a good idea.
mistakes.right: I think this is a good idea.
mistakes.why: Think = opinion: a state.

mistakes.wrong: What do you think about? You look worried.
mistakes.right: What are you thinking about? You look worried.
mistakes.why: Think = consider: an action.

mistakes.wrong: This soup is tasting delicious.
mistakes.right: This soup tastes delicious.
mistakes.why: Taste = the flavour it has: a state.

points.title: He's being rude: be in the continuous, and states in perfect tenses
points.summary: is being + adjective = behaviour right now; state verbs stay simple in perfect tenses (I've known, not I've been knowing).

blocks.md: *Be* is normally a state: *He **is** rude* = that's his character. But *be* + adjective in the continuous describes **behaviour at the moment**: *He**'s being** rude* = he is behaving rudely now (maybe that's not normal for him).
We only do this with adjectives about behaviour: *silly, rude, kind, careful, patient, difficult, quiet.* Not with things you can't control: *He's tall* (not *He's being tall*).

The same rule applies to **perfect continuous** tenses: use the perfect simple with state verbs: *I**'ve known** him for years.* (not *I've been knowing*) *They **had owned** the house for twenty years.* (not *had been owning*)

examples.text: You**'re being** very quiet today. Is everything OK?
Stop it! You**'re being** silly.
She**'s** a very patient person.
I**'ve known** Sam since primary school.
We **had** only **had** the car for a month when it broke down.

mistakes.wrong: I've been knowing her for years.
mistakes.right: I've known her for years.
mistakes.why: Know is a state: perfect simple.

mistakes.wrong: He's being tall for his age.
mistakes.right: He's tall for his age.
mistakes.why: Being + adjective is only for behaviour.

points.title: State verbs in the continuous for emphasis or change
points.summary: Informally, some state verbs take the continuous to stress a temporary feeling or a gradual change: We're loving it, I'm regretting it.

blocks.md: With some state verbs, the continuous is possible to stress that a situation is **temporary or around now**: *The kids **are loving** their new school.* *You**'re looking** great these days.* This is common in informal English.

With verbs of **mental states** (*regret, realise, understand, find*), the continuous can show a feeling that is **growing or new**: *I**'m regretting** my decision more every day. I**'m** slowly **understanding** how the system works.* *Consider* (= think about carefully) is usually continuous: *He**'s considering** a move to Vancouver.*

Some verbs are still very rarely continuous, even informally: *believe, doubt, own, belong, consist of, know.* In exams and formal writing, use the simple form with state verbs unless you have a clear reason not to.

examples.text: We**'re loving** our new flat!
You**'re looking** great these days.
I**'m regretting** that I said yes.
He**'s considering** early retirement.
We**'re hoping** to finish by Friday.

mistakes.wrong: I'm believing you now.
mistakes.right: I believe you now.
mistakes.why: Believe is very rarely continuous.

mistakes.wrong: This box is consisting of three parts.
mistakes.right: This box consists of three parts.
mistakes.why: Consist of is never continuous.
